Synopsis:
All guards at the checkpoint point the player to the guard with this dialog. He is an evil, nasty character who has no reason to go easy on the player. Should ooze disdain. This is the first goblin we meet and their weasly, cruel, wicked nature should stand out.
The goblin will let a non-allied player in only if they smear worg shit on their face. Yuck.

Cluster Contexts:
- GOB_Checkpoint_Guard001.json: You arrive at the goblin checkpoint and are funneled to Sentinel Olak — the first goblin you meet — a sneering, cruel sentry accompanied by a worg (Klaw). Olak delights in humiliating outsiders: he insists non‑allied visitors smear steaming worg dung across their faces as the camp’s “war colours,” and taunts them that they can either do it or die. His tone is icy and contemptuous, not inclined to mercy; only someone openly recognised as a True Soul or otherwise granted favour would likely avoid the ritual. Off‑screen the camp is tense (raids, interrogations and goblin/drow leadership nearby), which explains why guards are vicious and quick to threaten.
- GOB_Checkpoint_Guard004.json: Goblin grunt guarding a checkpoint. Laconic; gruff.
- GOB_Checkpoint_Guard003.json: A goblin grunt guarding a checkpoint. Squirrely, animalian type. Friendlier than most, but not extremely friendly.
- GOB_GuardTense.json: This goblin is standing guard inside temple - he's a little more relaxed than his zealous companion. Offers 'beginners' advice to player. As hostile as any other goblin if you try to pass without his superior's permission.
- GOB_Checkpoint_Guard002.json: One of several goblin guards protecting a checkpoint. Grunt type who thinks he's more important than he is. If you humiliate yourself before him, he's gleeful in your misery.

context: You approach a goblin checkpoint where all the other sentries funnel outsiders to Sentinel Olak — the first goblin you meet — a sneering, weasly sentry with a worg called Klaw at his side. Olak delights in humiliating outsiders: he greedily points to a steaming pile of worg dung and insists non‑allied visitors smear it on their faces as the camp’s “war colours,” offering compliance or death; only someone openly recognised as a True Soul (or otherwise granted favour) is likely to skip the ritual. Off‑screen the camp is tense from recent raids and interrogations and goblin/drow leadership is nearby, which helps explain the guards’ icy, vicious enforcement. In the example exchanges the player and companions debate complying, refuse, or retaliate while Olak taunts and savors their misery.
